candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXXV.10. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And God said unto him, Thy name is Jacob: thy name shall not be called any more Jacob, but Israel shall be thy name'. Ephrem notes the divine reconfirmation: the angelic Jabbok name-change is now RATIFIED by God Himself in direct theophany. The pattern of double-confirmation (angelic-then-divine) is preserved in Tewahedo sacramental practice: the deacon's prayer precedes the priest's consecration; the bishop's chrismation ratifies the presbyter's baptism. Authority moves in stages, never bypassed.

candidates.source_name: Ephrem the Syrian / Commentary on Genesis
candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXXV.18. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And it came to pass, as her soul was in departing, (for she died,) that she called his name Ben-oni: but his father called him Benjamin'. Ephrem reads the double-naming as the dialectic of grief-and-hope: the mother dying names her son Son-of-my-sorrow; the father renames him Son-of-the-right-hand (i.e., Son-of-strength / favoured-son). Tewahedo pastoral theology preserves this pattern: the church speaks both griefs honestly AND reframes them into hope, never denying the first.
